draft.title: Australian overseas aid
card: Overseas aid is money, goods, skills and services that one country gives to another to improve wellbeing. The Australian Government pays for Australia's aid from its budget.
Most of Australia's aid goes to countries in the Indo-Pacific region, which includes Southeast Asia and the Pacific islands. These are close neighbours, and many have lower incomes.
Aid is spent on health, education, infrastructure and disaster recovery. Examples are vaccination programs, school teacher training, roads and ports, and rebuilding after a cyclone.
Aid is one way to lift wellbeing in other countries. It is given by a government, so it is different from money raised by charities.
draft.remember: Australian aid is government support, mostly to Asia and the Pacific, for health, education, infrastructure and recovery.

a.q: Which of these is an example of Australian overseas aid?
opts: The Australian Government funds a hospital in Vanuatu
A charity runs a sponsor-a-child appeal in Australia
A Queensland council builds a new local swimming pool
An Australian company opens a factory in Indonesia
a.why: Overseas aid is given by the Australian Government to another country to improve wellbeing, and a hospital in Vanuatu fits this. A charity appeal is tempting, but charities are not the government, so it is not Australian Government aid.
a.clue: Who gives the aid, and where does it go?

b.q: After a cyclone hits an island nation in the Pacific, the Australian Government pays to rebuild damaged roads and bridges. Which type of aid is this?
opts: Infrastructure and disaster recovery
Health and education only
Aid given by a charity
Spending on Australian roads
b.why: Roads and bridges are infrastructure, and rebuilding after a cyclone is disaster recovery, so this aid fits both. It is not aid by a charity, because the Australian Government pays for it.
b.clue: Think about what is being rebuilt, and why.

a.best: The Australian Government funds a hospital in Vanuatu
